From Stars to STEM

By: Anina Peens | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Imagine running with the Wildebees or seeing the inside of a vulcano. We take you there!

Unique Selling Point:
Journey from the depths of a human blood vessel to the heart of a thundering Serengeti migration, and witness a collapsing glacier up close—this is not just a story, it’s a revolution in how we see and understand our world. The Wits Dome, once a historic planetarium, is reborn as a groundbreaking digital masterpiece. Join us as we uncover the awe, the history, and the future of this one-of-a-kind experience

Summary:
From long queues to witness Halley’s Comet and the moon landing in the 1960s to today’s 8K immersive journeys through the Serengeti or the human brain, South Africa’s first planetarium has always been a gateway to discovery. Now reborn as the Wits Anglo American Digital Dome, this iconic space blends six decades of history with cutting-edge technology to redefine education and bring the world—and beyond—to Johannesburg.

Further information:
Background
In 1960, the Johannesburg Planetarium opened its doors as Africa’s first full-sized planetarium, quickly becoming a symbol of scientific curiosity and educational innovation. Within its first decade, over one million visitors marvelled at its ability to bring the cosmos to life. It was a time when South Africans lined up to see Halley’s Comet and formed queues around the block to experience the moon landing. For generations, the Planetarium ignited a passion for learning and exploration that shaped countless lives.
Today, after an ambitious R90-million transformation, the Planetarium has been reborn as the Wits Anglo American Digital Dome. This state-of-the-art facility is the largest of its kind in the southern hemisphere, equipped with 10 digital projectors rendering an 8K full-dome resolution and an 8.2 audio system for a fully immersive experience.
But the Dome is more than a technological marvel—it’s a game-changer for STEM education, research, and beyond. Visitors can journey inside the human brain, explore the Serengeti migration, or view the Northern Lights—all from Johannesburg. For researchers, it provides a space to visualize complex data, from engineering prototypes to astrophysics simulations. The Dome is poised to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and artists, just as it did decades ago.
What makes this story even more remarkable is the people behind it. One staff member has been part of the Planetarium’s journey since its opening in 1960, offering a unique perspective on how it has evolved from a stargazing icon to a multidisciplinary hub of innovation.
This transformation isn’t just about cutting-edge technology—it’s about continuing a legacy of inspiring curiosity, fostering education, and making science accessible to all South Africans. As the Dome prepares to open its doors to the public in February 2025, it marks the beginning of a new era for how we explore and understand the world around us.

Script:


WITS PLANETARIUM FINAL

UPS Archive: 10, 9. Ignition sequence starts…
VO
The 1960’s…the height of the Space Race.
UPS Archive: It’s one small step for man…”
VO
As the United States and the Soviet Union vied for dominance over the stars, the world watched history unfold.
UPS Archive: a giant leap for mankind…
VO
For South Africans, it was the Johannesburg Planetarium that opened a window onto the cosmos.
CONSTANT VOLSCHENK: In the center, they put up a bunch of TVs… The tapes were recorded in the UK, flown to South Africa, and brought immediately into the dome to show it… and the queues was standing here from the front door into De Korte Street.
VO
For generations, the dome drew over a million visitors a year. And at its heart stood a German pioneer—the Mark 3 Zeiss projector.
For Supervisor, Constant Volschenk, the projector was more than just a machine…
For over 60 years, displaying over 8,000 stars—it was a storyteller and a teacher.
CONSTANT VOLSCHENK: It’s a different instrument. You could, if you’re tired working in the office, you could come to it, put on some music, cleaning it, which we had to do because it leaked oil.

VO:
But in 2022, the old guardian cast its final beam.

CONSTANT VOLSCHENK: It became static - that’s why we had to change.

VO:
Now, the dome is lighting up again, ready to enthrall a new generation of visitors.

FADE TO BLACK

DR MOUMITA AICH: As a child, the first time I saw Saturn through a telescope, I think I still have it imprinted in my memory…and I can still see it.

VO
Moumita Aich has always had her head in the stars.

DR MOUMITA AICH: I grew up in Kolkata in India. I was always interested in astronomy because maybe we didn’t have that much pollution at that time in India. And, we used to see all these meteor showers happening,
VO
Today she’s a cosmologist heading the oldest full-sized Planetarium on the African continent.

UPSOUND IN DOME DR MOUMITA AICH: Just do a timelapse for me… Yeah, okay that works.


VO
The refurbished dome’s state-of-the-art digital projection system … offers a fully immersive experience…
UPS Dome Show: One of the obvious… one over here!
VO
Dr. Aich’s ambition for the new dome is to change the future of education.

UPS Moumita Aich in Dome: Orion there.. The Hunter…

DR MOUMITA AICH: It is a place for research as well as teaching. So people can actually bring in… even University students, they can come here and they have all these modules which are on science or art, or architecture. And you can also do your own content to be put on this dome. So, these are things we also try to focus on rather than just coming here for just a show. But these are also aspects we’re trying to bring out to the public.

VO
Using real data and artificial intelligence, the dome can transport visitors from the depths of the ocean to the heart of the International Space Station.

CONSTANT VOLSCHENK: This is actual factual content, from astronomical databases. It is real.

UPSOUND Dome Show: Are you guys ready? Yeah! Okay!
UPSOUND Dome Show: We don’t have to worry about another planet colliding with earth…

DR MOUMITA AICH: There’s a lot of cool stuff happening within South Africa in astronomy and with the dome you can do so many interesting things. Just to look at Saturn, it looks amazing.

CONSTANT VOLSCHENK: We’ve got thousands of kids coming through the planetarium. If it could just trigger one of them to go into the sciences, or even into engineering then I think the job is done…
DR MOUMITA AICH: All these projects doesn't only require astronomers, they require engineers, they require technicians. And I think the dome will motivate people to see it as potential career for them.



PROMO 1

How did the historic planetarium transform into a cutting edge digital masterpiece that could redefine education? Discover the story behind the dome….
UPS
Prepare to witness the stars like never before!

PROMO 2
What connects a retired German projector, decades of wonder and a revolutionary new way to explore the universe? The answer lies inside this dome…
UPS
We venture into the unknown in full colour high definition.
